newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Cash-strapped Russia delays space station launch.
newsitem.headline: Cash-strapped Russia delays space station launch.

text.p: Russia, struggling for cash for its troubled space programme, has postponed the launch of the first module of the Alpha international space station, casting new doubts over Moscow's ability to participate in the project.

Yuri Koptev, head of the Russian Space Agency, told a news conference on Monday that the module would be launched in June next year, rather than this November. The delay this would cause to the international project was Russia's fault.
"The timetable will be changed because of Russia, which did not build a service module on time," he said.

The new space station, to be complete by 2003, is being funded by Russia, the United States, the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan. Russia is building the first module, a cargo section, and the third, a service area where cosmonauts will live and work.

Some U.S. officials already say Moscow, which also blames cash shortages for long delays in building the third module, is not pulling its weight. A delay in launching the first module will also delay launch of the second stage, a docking module being built in the United States.
After the third module, other parts of the station will be attached in stages by 2003.

"The problem is with the service module, which if not finished on time will unravel the whole project," James Sensenbrenner, chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives' Science Committee, said last week. Sensenbrenner is a fierce critic of Russia's contribution to the Alpha project.
Alpha will cost a total of $37 billion and will replace Russia's ageing Mir orbiting station, where cosmonauts extinguished a small fire in an air filtering unit on Sunday.
It was the latest in a series of minor mishaps aboard Mir, which was launched in 1985 and has already outlasted its expected lifespan.

Six cosmonauts -- four Russians, one American and one German -- are currently aboard the station. An official with Russia's military space forces said the blaze was "not a serious incident" and that it had been put out in seven minutes.
"There was no need to evacuate the Mir crew," he said.
Toilet tanks on Mir overflowed last year after delays in bringing supplies to the station, and a new generator was hastily flown to the station after problems with energy supplies.
The blaze highlighted the problems facing the Russian space centre, which was the jewel of the Soviet industrial crown, but which has suffered years of underfunding and wage delays.

"Forty two percent of our top specialists have left the space industry in the last five years," Koptev said. "Only 14 space enterprises have paid wages without delay. We owe the federal budget 220 billion roubles ($40 million)."
He said state financing of the space sector was just one seventh of that in Soviet days, but cooperation with foreign firms was now offering domestic companies a lifeline worth millions of dollars.
This cooperation, including the lucrative business of sending Western cosmonauts to Mir, now earned Russian companies $471 million a year compared with $20 million in 1992, he said.
Koptev said Russian space experts supported the Alpha project because it would help develop the Russian space programme. "We do not have an alternative," he said.
